doc.title: Jason Palmer interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 2, 2025

title: Energy on the bandstand: Clifford Brown and enjoying the stage
summary: Palmer finds players who do not enjoy themselves disappointing and recalls the Max Roach story about Clifford Brown.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Is there anything on the bandstand that you’ve either observed or experienced that you find aggravating?

You know at this point in my life just seeing people that aren’t enjoying themselves on the bandstand. That’s probably the most general answer I can give to that. You know or somebody that’s just not giving energy. You know I think energy is something — you can feel it, you can hear it, and you know it when it’s not there. I always hearken back to this story that I think Max Roach told about Clifford Brown where after a concert a lady came up to him, came up to Clifford and said, “You know I don’t know what you played tonight but you sure played the hell out of it.” You know? And so I’ve always tried to live on the bandstand with that kind of thing. Because you never know, Clifford died when he was 25 you know, and so everything we have of him, you could sense that he was really playing in a way where it was just reckless abandon. He was going to play his best at all times. He never really dialed it in. I can’t detect any dialing in in his playing. And so when I hear players that I know and admire and, you know, come to expect something like that from, you know I mean it’s disappointing. I wouldn’t say aggravating, but yeah, probably disappointing. That plus as I said before, not enjoying being on stage. I think even as an audience member, you know you don’t want to look like your not having a good time. You know the music’s already dense enough, and to see somebody up there you know not really into it you know that’s a drag. Especially if it’s a gig where you like paid to go see a band and you know everybody’s like this. You know play the solo and then go to the side like this. Like snap your finger a little bit. You know, get into it. Cheer your band on. Sometimes they need an uplift and they need a little yeah, something to get them inspired. You know? And you know I’ve had people come up to me and they’ll say, “You really looked like you were enjoying yourself up there, I really enjoyed that.” You know? They might not have understood the sharp nines I played on every chord or whatnot, but they say, “Yeah I really enjoyed that, you all looked like you © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-
were having fun up there. You sound like you were a band.” And we need more of that. Every band needs to do that.

You just reminded me of the last time I did adjudicating at a high school festival and we were required to go up and talk to the band afterwards. And I went up and I said, “You know the band sounds great, it’s okay for you to smile.” All the students were so like serious and there was no acknowledgement of their fellow band members when they got up to solo or anything. I said, “You’ve got to like loosen up.” And as you said, it’s contagious.
The audience is going to like your band better if you do that. They may not even know why.
